title: The Clear Offer Checklist: The 10-Second Stranger Test for Your Cold Email
description: Can a stranger repeat your offer in one sentence? The 10-second test, a one-sentence offer formula and a checklist to make cold email offers clear.
lead: This is the full setup checklist from the reel. You get the 10-second stranger test, a one-sentence offer formula, before-and-after examples, a word-cutting table, a problem finder and a prompt that rewrites your offer for you.
insider: Before any client campaign goes out, we cut the offer down until a stranger can say it back in one sentence. For one agency client, that clear offer was sent to the right people from June 1 to October 19, 2026: **82,671 emails brought 2,429 replies, and 88% of them were positive**, 2,146 people saying "yes, tell me more." The clear sentence is the easy part; the full system (list, inboxes, follow-ups) is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: The short answer

Ask a stranger to repeat what you do in one sentence. If they can say it back, your offer works. If they can't, rewrite it. That's the whole test. It takes 10 seconds and it catches the most common reason good cold emails get ignored.

Your email can reach the inbox and still fail. If the reader can't tell in a few seconds **who it's for** and **what they get**, they won't reply. They won't ask you to explain either. They just move on.
Why a clear offer gets more replies

**Readers decide fast.** [Instantly's 2026 benchmark report](https://instantly.ai/cold-email-benchmark-report-2026) found the top senders, with reply rates 2 to 4 times the average, write first emails **under 80 words** with **one clear call to action** and lead with the reader's problem. There's no room in 80 words for an offer that takes three sentences to explain.

**Unclear reads as irrelevant or salesy.** In [Hunter's State of Email Outreach 2026](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email), **65% of decision makers** said cold emails fail because they feel too sales-focused, and **61%** said they fail because they aren't relevant. A vague offer full of big words hits both: the reader can't see that it's for them, and it sounds like a pitch.

**One clear ask wins.** Instantly says multiple calls to action dilute focus, and top performers use simple questions like "Worth a quick call?" Hunter found decision makers prefer soft asks like "Open to learning more?" over booking a meeting upfront. A clear offer makes a small ask easy to say yes to.
The 10-second stranger test

items: Write your offer as **one sentence**. No commas doing the work of three sentences.
Find someone who doesn't know your business: a friend, a family member, a person in another industry.
Read the sentence to them **once**. Don't explain it.
Ask: "Can you tell me in your own words what I do and who it's for?"
**Pass:** they name the right buyer and the right result. **Fail:** they guess, hesitate, or ask "so what do you actually do?"
If it fails, rewrite with the formula below and test again with a new person (the first one now knows the answer).

blocks.label: No stranger nearby?
blocks.text: Use the prompt at the end of this page. It's not as good as a real person, but it catches jargon and missing parts fast.
The setup checklist
The four steps from the reel. Each has the why, then exactly how.
Step 1: Say who it's for
**Why:** a reader only replies if they see themselves in the email. "Businesses" is nobody. "Roofing companies in Texas" is someone.

items: Name the buyer by **industry or type**: dental clinics, B2B SaaS founders, IT agencies.
Add **one detail** that narrows it: size, location or situation ("with 5 to 20 staff", "that just raised a seed round").
Use the words your buyer uses for themselves, not the words you use about them.

blocks.text: Step 2: Say the one result they get
**Why:** buyers pay for results, not for your process. If you list five results, the reader remembers none.

items: Pick the **one** result your best clients care about most.
Make it something they can see or count: more booked calls, fewer no-shows, faster invoices.
Only add a number if you can prove it. A made-up number destroys trust the moment they check.

blocks.text: Step 3: Use plain words a stranger would repeat
**Why:** people can only repeat words they understand. If your sentence needs a glossary, it fails the test.

head: Cut this
Say this instead
rows: Fix how you [follow up / send invoices]

blocks.text: Step 4: Cut everything else
**Why:** every extra word is one more thing the reader has to skip to find the point. Keep the offer, cut the rest.

items: Cut your company history, awards and founding story from the first email.
Cut the full service list. Pick the one thing this list of buyers needs.
Cut "I hope this finds you well" and other filler before the offer (our [opener swap sheet](/guides/well.html) has replacements).
Keep **one** ask at the end.

blocks.text: The one-sentence offer formula

blocks.label: Fill in the blanks
blocks.text: We help [who it's for] get [one result] without [the pain they hate].
The last part is optional. Use it only if it's short and real. If your sentence is longer than about 20 words, you're explaining, not offering.
Worked example: before and after

head: Version
Offer
Stranger test
rows: We are a full-service growth partner that leverages data-driven, end-to-end outbound solutions, including list building, copywriting, deliverability optimization and CRM integration, to help ambitious B2B organizations across multiple verticals unlock scalable, predictable revenue growth and maximize their sales pipeline potential.
We help B2B agencies with 5 to 50 staff get booked sales calls without running ads.

blocks.text: Count it: the before version is **40 words** in one sentence. The after version is **16 words**. The after version also passes Steps 1 to 4: it names the buyer (B2B agencies with 5 to 50 staff), one result (booked sales calls), the pain they hate (running ads), and nothing else.
Here's the after version inside a full first email, still well under 80 words:

blocks.label: Example first email (64 words)
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

We help B2B agencies with 5 to 50 staff get booked sales calls without running ads.

Most agencies we talk to get new clients from referrals, which is great until a few months go quiet.

We set up cold email that books calls every week, and we do the work.

Open to seeing how it would work for [company]?

[Your name]

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Testing on a colleague.** They already know what you do. Use a real stranger.
**Explaining after you read it.** If you have to add "what I mean is...", it failed.
**One offer for every buyer.** Different lists need different "who" and "result" lines.
**Clever over clear.** A smart-sounding line nobody can repeat loses to a plain one everybody can.
**Adding numbers you can't prove.** Clear and true beats big and made up.

blocks.text: Rewrite your offer with Claude

blocks.label: Clear offer prompt
blocks.text:
Act as a stranger who knows nothing about my business, then as a cold email editor.

My current offer: [paste your offer or first email]
Who I sell to: [industry, size, location]
The one result my best clients get: [result]
Proof I can actually show: [real numbers or results, or "none yet"]

Do this:
1) As the stranger, repeat what I do in one sentence, in your own words. Say honestly if you can't.
2) List every word a stranger might not understand or would not repeat.
3) Write 5 versions using: "We help [who] get [one result] without [pain]." Each under 20 words, plain words only.
4) Do not invent numbers or results. Only use the proof I gave you.
5) Pick the clearest version and write a first cold email under 80 words with one soft question at the end.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: If a stranger can't say it back, your buyer won't either. Rewrite until they can.

faq.q: Who counts as a stranger for the test?
faq.a: Anyone who doesn't know your business and isn't in your industry. A friend, a neighbor or a family member works. Don't use a teammate or a client; they already know the answer.

faq.q: Should my offer include a number?
faq.a: Only if you can prove it with a real result. A clear offer without a number beats a big number the reader doesn't believe.

faq.q: Can I have different offers for different buyers?
faq.a: Yes, and you should. Write one sentence per list. A dental clinic and a SaaS founder want different results, so they need different "who" and "result" lines.

faq.q: My offer passes, but nobody replies. Now what?
faq.a: Then the offer probably isn't the problem. Check that you're emailing the right people and that your emails reach the inbox. Our [deliverability checklist](/guides/inbox.html) covers the checks.
